text: Then one Saturday, we went to his village to visit. <break time="0.8s" /> And his mother showed us a beautifully patterned basket, made of dyed raffia, that his brother had made. <break time="0.8s" /> I was startled. <break time="0.8s" /> It had not occurred to me that anybody in his family could actually make something. <break time="0.8s" /> All I had heard about them was how poor they were, so that it had become impossible for me to see them as anything else but poor. <break time="0.8s" /> Their poverty was my single story of them. <break time="0.8s" /> Years later, I thought about this when I left Nigeria to go to university in the United States. <break time="0.8s" /> I was 19. <break time="0.8s" /> My American roommate was shocked by me. <break time="0.8s" /> She asked where I had learned to speak English so well, and was confused when I said that Nigeria happened to have English as one of its official languages. <break time="0.8s" /> She asked if she could listen to what she called my tribal music, and was consequently very disappointed when I produced my tape of Mariah Carey. <break time="0.8s" /> She assumed that I did not know how to use a stove. <break time="0.8s" /> What struck me was this, she had felt sorry for me even before she saw me. <break time="0.8s" /> Her default position toward me, as an African, was a kind of patronizing, well meaning, pity. <break time="0.8s" /> My roommate had a single story of Africa. <break time="0.8s" /> A single story of catastrophe. <break time="0.8s" /> In this single story there was no possibility of Africans being similar to her, in any way. <break time="0.8s" /> No possibility of feelings more complex than pity. <break time="0.8s" /> No possibility of a connection as human equals. <break time="0.8s" /> I must say that before I went to the U, S, I did not consciously identify as African. <break time="0.8s" /> But in the U, S, whenever Africa came up, people turned to me. <break time="0.8s" /> Never mind that I knew nothing about places like Namibia.
